This happens for example when actual = 42f and expected = 42d, which will give this error:  actual : "42" and expected : "42".  JUnit 4 manages this case even worst, it will output something like :  "java.lang.String expected:java.lang.String<42.0> but was: java.lang.String<42.0>"  which makes things even more confusing since we lost the fact that 42 was a float or a double. records.raw_text: When comparing 42f with 42d, assertion error messages can be misleading—both display as "42," obscuring their type difference. Building a custom description without using ComparisonFailure resolves this ambiguity, though the output won't format as nicely in IDEs.

This happens for example when actual = 42f and expected = 42d, which will give this error:  actual : "42" and expected : "42".  JUnit 4 manages this case even worst, it will output something like :  "java.lang.String expected:java.lang.String<42.0> but was: java.lang.String<42.0>"  which makes things even more confusing since we lost the fact that 42 was a float or a double. records.raw_text: When comparing floating-point values of different types (e.g., actual = 42f, expected = 42d), assertion outputs create confusion: both values display identically as "42," obscuring the critical type difference between float and double. JUnit 4 compounds this problem by showing both as "42.0," further obscuring important type information in the output. Building a custom assertion description without using ComparisonFailure resolves this issue completely, though the trade-off is that IDE formatting and presentation will be less polished in test failure reports.
